questions.prompt: What is the impedance of an ideal capacitor C at angular frequency \(\omega\)?
questions.explanation:
From I \(=j\omega C\cdot V\) (reader Eq. 2.26), \(Z_{C}=V/I=1/(j\omega C)=-j/(\omega C)\). It is purely imaginary, with magnitude \(1/(\omega C)\) that shrinks as frequency rises.
• \(j\omega C\) is the ADMITTANCE \(Y_{C}\), not the impedance.
• \(-j\omega C\) has the wrong dependence on \(\omega\) (it would grow with frequency).
• \(C/(j\omega)\) has wrong units.

questions.prompt: In sinusoidal steady state, how do an ideal capacitor and an ideal inductor behave as \(\omega\to 0\) (near DC)?
options: The capacitor acts like a short circuit; the inductor acts like an open circuit
The capacitor acts like an open circuit; the inductor acts like a short circuit
questions.explanation: \(|Z_{C}|=1/(\omega C)\to\infty\) as \(\omega\to 0\) (open circuit), and \(|Z_{L}|=\omega L\to 0\) (short circuit). At very high frequency the roles reverse: the capacitor shorts and the inductor opens.

questions.prompt: What is the magnitude of the impedance of a 100 nF capacitor at \(f=1\ \mathrm{kHz}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(|Z_{C}|=1/(\omega C)=1/(2\pi\times 1000\times 100\times 10^{-9})=1/(6.283\times 10^{-4})=1592\ \Omega\).
Common mistake: using f instead of \(\omega\ (1/(1000\times 10^{-7})=10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega)\).

questions.prompt: A 300 Ω resistor is in series with a 40 mH inductor. What is the magnitude of the total impedance at \(\omega=10{,}000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(Z=R+j\omega L=300+j(10^{4}\times 0.04)=300+j400\ \Omega\).
\(|Z|=\sqrt{300^{2}+400^{2}}=\sqrt{250}{,}000=500\ \Omega\) (a 3-4-5 triangle).
Common mistake: adding magnitudes, \(300+400=700\ \Omega\). Resistance and reactance are 90° apart in the complex plane, so they add as vectors.

questions.prompt: A 0.1 µF capacitor has the voltage \(v(t)=5\cos(2\pi\cdot 1000\cdot t)\ \mathrm{V}\) across it. What is the PEAK value of the current through it?
questions.explanation:
Phasor relation: I \(=j\omega C\cdot V\), so \(|I|=\omega C|V|=2\pi(1000)(0.1\times 10^{-6})(5)=3.142\ \mathrm{mA}\).
(The current leads the voltage by 90°.) Common mistake: forgetting \(2\pi\), which gives 0.5 mA.

questions.prompt: For a single circuit element, the voltage is \(v(t)=10\cos(\omega t)\ \mathrm{V}\) and the current is \(i(t)=2\cos(\omega t-90^{\circ})\) A with \(\omega=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). What is the element?
questions.explanation:
The current LAGS the voltage by 90°, which is the signature of an inductor (\(V=j\omega L\cdot I\), so V leads I by 90°). \(|Z|=10\ \mathrm{V}/2\) A \(=5\ \Omega=\omega L\) ⇒ \(L=5/1000=5\ \mathrm{mH}\).
• A capacitor's current would LEAD the voltage by 90°; 200 µF would have \(1/(\omega C)=5\ \Omega\) but the wrong phase relationship.
• A resistor would have current in phase with voltage.
• 5 H would make \(\omega L=5000\ \Omega\), not 5 Ω (units slip).
questions.figure_alt: Voltage cosine and a current cosine lagging it by 90 degrees.

questions.prompt: A series circuit of an inductor and a capacitor is driven by a sinusoidal source. The measured voltage amplitudes are \(|V_{L}|=40\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(|V_{C}|=30\ \mathrm{V}\). What is the amplitude of the source voltage?
questions.explanation:
In a series circuit the same current flows through both, so \(V_{L}=j\omega L\cdot I\) leads I by 90° and \(V_{C}=I/(j\omega C)\) lags I by 90°: the two voltages are 180° out of phase and subtract. Source \(=|40-30|=10\ \mathrm{V}\) (phasor addition, reader Fig. 2.12).
• 70 V adds the magnitudes as if they were in phase.
• 50 V is the Pythagorean sum \((\sqrt{40^{2}+30^{2}})\), which would be right if they were 90° apart (e.g., one was a resistor voltage).
• 35 V is just their average.

questions.prompt: A 10 µF capacitor has \(v(t)=20\cos(1000t)\ \mathrm{V}\) across it (t in seconds). What is the current \(i(t)\) at \(t=1\ \mathrm{ms}\)? (Use the reference direction that makes \(i=C\cdot dv/dt\).)
questions.explanation:
Phasor: I \(=j\omega C\cdot V=j(1000)(10\times 10^{-6})(20)=j0.2\) A \(=0.2\angle 90^{\circ}\) A. So \(i(t)=0.2\cos(1000t+90^{\circ})=-0.2\ \sin(1000t)\) A.
At \(t=1\ \mathrm{ms}\): \(\omega t=1\ \mathrm{rad}\), so \(i=-0.2\ \sin(1\ \mathrm{rad})=-0.2\times 0.8415=-168.3\ \mathrm{mA}\).
(Check with the time-domain relation \(i=C\ dv/dt=10\ \mu\mathrm{F}\times(-20000\ \sin(1000t))=-0.2\ \sin(1000t)\) A ✔.)
Common mistakes: working in degrees \((\sin 1^{\circ}=0.0175)\) or dropping the 90° phase lead \((0.2\cos(1)=+108\ \mathrm{mA})\).

questions.prompt: Using a cosine reference, which phasor represents \(v(t)=10\sin(\omega t+30^{\circ})\ \mathrm{V}\)?
questions.explanation:
Phasors are defined relative to \(\cos(\omega t+\phi)\). Convert: \(\sin(x)=\cos(x-90^{\circ})\), so \(10\sin(\omega t+30^{\circ})=10\cos(\omega t+30^{\circ}-90^{\circ})=10\cos(\omega t-60^{\circ})\). The phasor is \(10\angle-60^{\circ}\).
• \(10\angle 30^{\circ}\) treats the sine as a cosine (no conversion).
• \(10\angle 120^{\circ}\) adds 90° instead of subtracting it (that would represent \(-\sin\)).
• \(10\angle 60^{\circ}\) flips the sign of the correct phase.

questions.prompt: Preview of finding \(H(j\omega)\) directly. A later skill shows that a series R–L circuit with the output taken across the inductor has \(H(j\omega)=j\omega L/(R+j\omega L)\). With \(R=1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\), \(L=10\ \mathrm{mH}\), \(\omega=100\ \mathrm{krad}/\mathrm{s}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{in}}(t)=4\cos(\omega t)\ \mathrm{V}\), what is the steady-state output \(v_{\mathrm{out}}\) at \(t=0\)?
questions.explanation:
Phasor impedances: \(Z_{L}=j\omega L=j(10^{5})(0.01)=j1000\ \Omega\). \(H=j1000/(1000+j1000)=j/(1+j)=0.7071\angle(90^{\circ}-45^{\circ})=0.7071\angle 45^{\circ}\).
Output \(=4\times 0.7071=2.828\ \mathrm{V}\) amplitude with a +45° phase: \(v_{\mathrm{out}}=2.828\cos(\omega t+45^{\circ})\).
At \(t=0\): \(2.828\cos 45^{\circ}=2\ \mathrm{V}\).
Common mistake: using −45° (for a low-pass) or forgetting that an inductor's impedance is a positive-imaginary number.

questions.prompt: Preview of AC power. A later skill shows that the average power into a load is \(P=\tfrac{1}{2}|I|^{2}\cdot\mathrm{Re}\{Z\}\), where I is the peak current phasor. A load is a 10 Ω resistor in series with a capacitor whose reactance magnitude is 10 Ω at \(\omega=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\ (C=100\ \mu\mathrm{F})\). The peak current is 2 A. What is the average power?
questions.explanation:
\(Z=R+1/(j\omega C)=10-j10\ \Omega\), so \(\mathrm{Re}\{Z\}=10\ \Omega\) (the imaginary part comes from the capacitor).
\(P=\tfrac{1}{2}(2\ \mathrm{A})^{2}(10\ \Omega)=20\ \mathrm{W}\). The capacitor's reactance does not change the answer: only the resistive part dissipates power.
Common mistake: using \(|Z|=14.1\ \Omega\) (gives 28.3 W) or forgetting the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) for a peak (not RMS) current (40 W).

questions.prompt: Preview of series RLC circuits. A series circuit has \(R=50\ \Omega\), \(L=10\ \mathrm{mH}\) and \(C=1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\). (A later skill shows it resonates at \(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{LC}=10{,}000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), where \(\mathrm{Im}\ Z=0\).) What is the magnitude of the total impedance at \(\omega=5000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), half the resonant frequency?
questions.explanation:
\(Z=R+j\omega L+1/(j\omega C)\).
\(j\omega L=j(5000)(0.01)=+j50\ \Omega\). \(1/(j\omega C)=-j/(5000\times 10^{-6})=-j200\ \Omega\).
\(Z=50+j(50-200)=50-j150\ \Omega\).
\(|Z|=\sqrt{50^{2}+150^{2}}=\sqrt{25}{,}000=158.1\ \Omega\) (capacitive, since the capacitor's reactance dominates below resonance).
Common mistake: adding the reactances with the same sign \((50+200=250)\), or adding magnitudes of everything (300 Ω).
